o: For each seller, count the distinct items they sold whose brand differs from that seller's favorite brand; report everyone tied for the maximum count. Seller 2 sold items 4,1,4 — brands HP, Samsung, HP versus favorite Samsung — giving 1 distinct non-favorite item (item 4 counted once). We join Orders→Items→Users, filter mismatched brands, aggregate with COUNT(DISTINCT item_id), then keep only rows equal to the global max.
k: COUNT(DISTINCT item_id) handles duplicate orders of the same non-favorite item.
The tie handling needs a comparison against MAX over all sellers, conveniently done with a window function or a subquery.
Sellers with zero qualifying items should not appear (they cannot be the max unless everyone is 0 — constraints imply at least one match in practice).

a.n: Join, aggregate, then filter with a window/rank-free max comparison
a.i: Aggregate mismatches per seller in a CTE, then select rows whose count equals the overall maximum computed in a second CTE.
s: Join Orders, Items, Users; keep rows where item_brand <> favorite_brand.
Group by seller and count distinct item ids.
Compute the global max count and return tied sellers ordered by seller_id.

c.python:
-- MySQL
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT o.seller_id, COUNT(DISTINCT i.item_id) AS num_items
  FROM Orders o
  JOIN Items i ON o.item_id = i.item_id
  JOIN Users u ON u.seller_id = o.seller_id
  WHERE i.item_brand <> u.favorite_brand
  GROUP BY o.seller_id
),
mx AS (SELECT MAX(num_items) AS m FROM counts)
SELECT seller_id, num_items
FROM counts
WHERE num_items = (SELECT m FROM mx)
ORDER BY seller_id;

a.t: O(O log O) — joins plus aggregation dominate.
a.sp: O(S) — one row per seller in the CTE.

w: Alternative: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY num_items DESC) = 1 achieves the same tie semantics. Pitfall: using COUNT(item_id) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT item_id) double-counts repeated orders (seller 2's duplicate item 4). Follow-up: restrict to orders after the seller joined, or per-brand breakdowns.
